title: Queryable Domain Attributes Hidden in Opaque Database Columns
pattern: Structured domain attributes or entity hierarchies are serialized (JSON, XML, comma-separated lists, binary blobs) into opaque generic columns, avoiding an appropriate schema and hiding values that need database-level querying, typing, or integrity.
why_bad: The database cannot validate types, index the hidden fields, enforce referential integrity, or answer targeted queries on them, so the application must scan whole tables, deserialize entire hierarchies to reach a single nested field, and carry fragile parser and error-handling logic itself.
detection: A generic text/blob column is decoded into domain attributes that require targeted querying, indexing, typing, or referential constraints. Two subcases: (a) application code reads a single column and immediately passes the raw string into a JSON/XML deserializer to populate domain-specific attributes, including repurposing an existing generic column (e.g., `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`) to avoid a formal schema migration; (b) relational table columns mapped to unstructured text or binary types hold serialized entity or value-collection hierarchies whose nested fields are filtered, joined, or constrained on.
counterexample: Small, self-contained values (e.g., key-value configurations) that are never used as query filters or constraint targets; document columns deliberately modeled as native JSON fields (e.g., PostgreSQL JSONB) with query and index behavior suited to the required operations. Consistent with owner-local value embedding: values read and changed only with their owner may be embedded when independent querying and constraints are unnecessary.
source: Release It!, "Adaptable Enterprise Architecture" [377, 781]; Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Chapter 2 [619]; *Implementing Domain-Driven Design (Vernon), Chapter 6, p. 225 [225]*
